title: Airports want govt to let international carriers spread their wings and shed protectionist stance
summary: Airport operators and industry bodies are urging the government to roll back protectionist constraints and allow international carriers greater operational freedom. They argue liberalisation would boost connectivity, tourism, competition and airport revenues while lowering airfares. Officials are asking for pragmatic, phased reforms that protect essential national interests while enabling growth.
content:
Airport operators and industry representatives are pressing the government to ease protectionist constraints on international carriers, arguing that a more liberal approach would strengthen connectivity, boost tourism and trade, and support lower fares for passengers. The calls come as airports seek to position themselves as enablers of broader economic growth rather than as protectors of market share for domestic airlines.

Executives and trade bodies say current bilateral limits, restrictive traffic rights and capacity constraints prevent foreign carriers from deploying more services and connecting passengers through Indian hubs. They contend that allowing international airlines to "spread their wings" would increase seat capacity, encourage competition, and attract more international transit traffic — all of which would benefit airports, ancillary services and the travelling public.

Airport operators also highlight the potential revenue upside from higher passenger volumes. Greater international connectivity typically drives higher retail, ground handling and cargo revenues at airports. Local economies around major hubs can benefit through increased tourism, business travel and cargo flows, reinforcing the argument for a calibrated opening of international services.

At the same time, industry voices acknowledge legitimate government concerns about protecting nascent domestic carriers and national strategic interests. They suggest a phased liberalisation approach that combines reciprocity, slot management, and safeguards for essential domestic services. Proposals on the table include carefully negotiated bilateral expansions, trial liberal routes, and regulatory tools to ensure fair competition and prevent abrupt market shocks.

Stakeholders stress that policy reform should be accompanied by improvements in infrastructure, slot allocation transparency and consumer protections. These complementary measures would help ensure that liberalisation translates into better outcomes for passengers and for the aviation ecosystem rather than merely shifting market dynamics.

The debate over opening up international routes is unfolding against a busy domestic transport backdrop. Recent industry developments include a cut in jet fuel prices, leadership changes at major carriers, weather-related travel advisories, and high-profile safety incidents involving trainer aircraft. Tribunal rulings on employee benefits at legacy carriers and local discussions about arrival fees at some airports add to the complex policy environment.

Airport executives say a constructive, evidence-based dialogue among government, regulators, airlines and airport operators is essential. They argue that with careful sequencing and protections, India can move toward a less protectionist aviation posture that supports connectivity, competition and the broader economy without abandoning legitimate regulatory objectives.
